content: Cefoxitin sodium is a second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that is administered parenterally. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of various serious infections caused by susceptible microorganisms. These include lower respiratory tract infections (such as pneumonia and lung abscess), urinary tract infections, intra-abdominal infections (e.g., peritonitis and intra-abdominal abscess), gynecological infections (e.g., endometritis, pelvic cellulitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease), septicemia, bone and joint infections, and skin and soft tissue infections. Cefoxitin is also used prophylactically to prevent infections in patients undergoing certain surgical procedures, such as gastrointestinal surgery, cesarean sections, and hysterectomies. Cefoxitin works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, which leads to bacterial cell death. It is effective against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including strains that produce beta-lactamases (penicillinases and cephalosporinases). However, it is not active against Chlamydia trachomatis, so additional anti-chlamydial therapy is required when treating pelvic inflammatory disease if this pathogen is suspected. Dosage and Administration For adults, the usual dosage ranges from 1 to 2 grams every 6 to 8 hours, depending on the severity of the infection, the susceptibility of the causative organism, and the patient’s condition. In patients with renal impairment, dosage adjustments are necessary. For surgical prophylaxis, a dose of 2 grams is typically administered intravenously 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure, with additional doses given postoperatively in some cases. In pediatric patients aged three months and older, the recommended dosage is 80 to 160 mg/kg/day, divided into 4 to 6 doses. The total daily dose should not exceed 12 grams. Cefoxitin is not recommended for use in neonates under three months of age due to insufficient safety and efficacy data. Contraindications and Warnings Cefoxitin is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to cephalosporins or any component of the formulation. Caution is advised in patients with a history of penicillin allergy, as cross-reactivity may occur. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefoxitin. This condition can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Adverse Reactions Cefoxitin is generally well-tolerated, but adverse reactions may occur. Common local reactions include thrombophlebitis at the injection site. Allergic reactions such as rash, urticaria, pruritus, and anaphylaxis have been reported. Gastrointestinal side effects include diarrhea, nausea, and pseudomembranous colitis. Rarely, cefoxitin may cause hematologic abnormalities (e.g., eosinophilia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), hepatic enzyme elevations, or renal dysfunction. Seizures have been reported, particularly in patients with renal impairment when the dosage was not appropriately reduced. Use in Special Populations Pregnancy: Cefoxitin is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies have not shown teratogenic effects, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Cefoxitin is excreted in low concentrations in human milk. Caution is advised when administering to breastfeeding women. Geriatric Patients: No significant differences in safety or efficacy have been observed in elderly patients compared to younger adults. However, because cefoxitin is primarily excreted by the kidneys, dose adjustments may be necessary in elderly patients with impaired renal function. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy have not been established in neonates under three months of age. In older pediatric patients, higher doses have been associated with an increased incidence of eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes. Drug Interactions Concomitant use of cefoxitin with aminoglycosides may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity. Cefoxitin and aminoglycosides should not be mixed in the same solution due to potential incompatibility, but they may be administered separately. Overdosage In cases of overdose, symptoms may include seizures, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Treatment involves discontinuation of the drug and supportive care. Hemodialysis may help remove cefoxitin from the bloodstream in cases of severe overdose. Storage and Stability Cefoxitin sodium should be stored in its dry state at temperatures between 2°C and 25°C (36°F to 77°F). Reconstituted solutions may darken over time, but this does not affect the drug’s potency. Patient Counseling Patients should be informed that cefoxitin is only effective against bacterial infections and does not treat viral infections such as the common cold. They should complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if symptoms improve, to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance. Patients should also be advised to report any severe diarrhea, as this may indicate C. difficile-associated colitis. Cefoxitin sodium is a valuable antibiotic for treating a wide range of infections, particularly those caused by beta-lactamase-producing bacteria. However, its use should be guided by susceptibility testing and clinical judgment to minimize the risk of resistance and adverse effects.
